newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico petrochemical sale attracts wary investors.
newsitem.headline: Mexico petrochemical sale attracts wary investors.

text.p: The Mexican government is once again extending a cordial invitation to foreigners to invest in state-owned petrochemical assets, but many companies are unsure whether they will reply.

After years of delays and infighting over the fate of the state-owned petrochemical assets, Energy Minister Jesus Reyes Heroles announced earlier this month a revised program to sell a 49 percent stake in the nation's 61 plants.
Foreigners can now also opt for full ownership in new petrochemical plants.
However, the previous plan to allow 100 percent foreign and private ownership of assets currently in state hands was ditched in the face of political opposition.
Such policy flip-flops have caused some foreign investors to revise their plans, according to Peter Spitz, director of New York-based Chem Systems Group.
"Mexico should, sooner or later, have a broad-scaled highly competitive petrochemical industry," he said in a speech at the eighteenth National Chemical Industry Forum Wednesday.
"But this will require a substantial investment, and that in turn will require an atmosphere where investors feel secure they can achieve a successful level of profitability."
Although many businessmen at the two-day conference expressed interest in owning a stake of Mexico's petrochemical industry, others expressed doubts.

"Buying no more than 49 percent (of a petrochemical) plant could be an advantage because it requires less capital," said Tadeo Perich, vice president of U.N. Petroquimica y Refineria in Argentina. "But a businessman is never going to want to cede control of his business."
Some foreign companies may be more patient than others, Reyes Heroles noted, as he told reporters the details for the petrochemical sale remain undefined.
The wait has delayed $1.06 billion of state investments destined for the nation's petrochemical units, he added.

"The new strategy undoubtedly presents a new situation compared to what was said a year ago and before, but (Shell) continues looking with interest at the possibility of strengthening its ties in Mexico and its petrochemicals," said Joaquin Moreno Uribe, president of Shell Mexico, subsidiary of Anglo-Dutch oil company Royal Dutch/Shell.
"We understand these processes of partial privatization are complex processes that take time." Other companies may not be so understanding.

"It has been the same for ten years and Pemex still lacks investment for exploring and technology," said Amado Cavazos, vice president of DuPont de Mexico, wholly-owned subsidiary of U.S.-based DuPont Co. Foreign businessmen who asked to remain anonymous said their companies are re-examining investment plans in light of the latest privatization restriction. Some expressed doubt competition would be fair between Pemex-owned petrochemical plants and new facilities owned by foreigners. Mexico's chemical industry accounted for 4 percent of gross domestic product in 1995, with production valued at $15 billion, according to National Chemical Industry President Raul Millares. --Mexico City newsroom 525 7287903
